abstract: Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman’s $\rho=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.

sections.body:
The introduction asks whether LLMs can advance theoretical computer science. It argues that the outcome on an unresolved conjecture alone reveals little about an LLM's research abilities. It identifies three research outputs: theorem proofs, solver programs, and constructions with verified properties.

TCSExam has 100 tasks: 20 research theorems in Lean 4, 30 solver problems, 20 construction problems, and 30 open conjectures in prove-or-refute form. Expert authors reviewed all 100 tasks. Every submission is checked by the Lean kernel or an executable checker. On the 20 theorems without supplied intermediate lemmas, GPT-6 Astra reaches a per-attempt complete-proof success rate of 70.0%.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Existing benchmarks cover parts of theoretical computer science, so TCSExam adds proofs, solvers, constructions, and open conjectures.

sections.body:
Related work covers formal and natural-language proof benchmarks, program search, and open-problem evaluations. TCS-BENCH uses an LLM verifier for natural-language proofs. The paper reports accuracy above 90% against expert judgments but no formal correctness guarantee. FormalTCS evaluates formalization and proving of TCS results, without reusable solver performance or construction quality.

AlphaTensor, AlphaDev, FunSearch, and AlphaEvolve use search or reinforcement learning for algorithms and improvements. FrontierCS 2 compares agent reimplementations across 48 public tasks. Formal Conjectures supplies formalized research problems and frozen evaluations. Table 1 marks TCSExam as the only benchmark checked in all four columns.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior benchmarks cover proofs, solvers, or conjectures separately, and only TCSExam covers all four.

sections.body:
TCSExam sorts tasks into four tracks by required output. Theorem tasks ask for a Lean 4 proof under bare, ladder, or guided context. Solver tasks take a reusable program scored over instance families. Construction tasks ask for an explicit object with a certificate, scored against documented records. Open-conjecture tasks accept a verified proof of either the statement or its negation.

The Index combines the four track means:

$$
I=30P+30S+30C+10O
$$

Here $P$, $S$, $C$, and $O$ are the theorem, solver, construction, and open-conjecture means. Lite keeps five tasks per track under the same scoring functions and weights.
sections.heading: TCSExam
sections.headline: TCSExam assigns each task to one of four tracks, each with its own required output and success criterion.

sections.body:
Each agent pairs an LLM with an execution harness. Full evaluates GPT-6 Astra, Kimi K3, GLM-5.3, Qwen3.8 Max (0902), Grok 4.6, two DeepSeek V4.1 Flash versions, and Kimi K3.1 Pro. Lite adds Opus 5.5. Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1 Pro, and both DeepSeek versions run three attempts per task; the others run one.

Theorem and solver development have no general Internet access. Construction and open-conjecture tasks allow literature access. Solver development uses online evaluation on Full and offline self-tests on Lite, with the same hidden-set judging. Attempts are averaged within tasks, and tasks are averaged equally within each track. A separate comparison runs Kimi K3 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 0910 on 20 theorems in three proof settings.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Eight agents run on Full and nine on Lite, each attempt limited to a 12-hour development budget.

sections.body:
**Full.** GPT-6 Astra completes 14 of 20 theorems (70.0%) and has an Index of 71.9. Kimi K3.1 Pro succeeds in 23 of 60 attempts (38.3%). Construction means range from 86.2% to 104.9%, with Astra highest. Astra's Solver relative score is 64.7%, where 50.0% equals the Kimi K3 reference mean.

**Lite and consistency.** Opus 5.5 has the highest Lite Index. Full and Lite agree on 26 of 28 pairs among eight shared agents, with $\rho=0.93$.

**Constructions and conjectures.** A submitted graph with 630 edges exceeds the 629-edge reference. Accepted Ryser and MIRUP submissions adapt published counterexamples. The other 28 conjecture tasks have no accepted complete solution.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: GPT-6 Astra leads Full with an Index of 71.9, and Opus 5.5 leads Lite with 72.3.

sections.body:
The conclusion presents TCSExam as a unified framework linking proving, solver engineering, constructions, and open-conjecture settlement. Full has 100 expert-reviewed tasks, checked by the Lean kernel or executable checkers. Lite keeps all four tracks in 20 tasks and reduces the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget.

The section states that results show complementary strengths in proof completion, solver performance, and construction quality. For both agents in the proof-guidance study, intermediate lemmas and proof ideas increase the number of theorems solved. It cites Astra's nine-dimensional Alon–Jaeger–Tarsi result over $\mathbb{F}_{5}$ as a verified open-conjecture attempt. It also notes that researchers can add problems through shared task interfaces.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The framework covers four research tracks, and Lite retains them while reducing attempts by 80%.

sections.body:
The statement says AI coding assistants were used in task authoring, formalization, checker implementation, and iterative review. AI assistants also supported data processing, result analysis, manuscript drafting and editing, figure code, and literature search.

Evaluated model outputs are identified as experimental submissions and checked under the relevant task protocol. Result tables and plots are generated programmatically from experiment records. The authors state that they take responsibility for the final content of the work.
sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.headline: AI assistants helped author tasks, build checkers, and draft text, and the authors take responsibility for the content.

sections.body:
Appendix A catalogues the 100 tasks by track. It lists 20 theorems with source papers and domains, 30 solver problems with sources and objectives, and 20 construction tasks with reference values. Later appendices give construction and open-conjecture results for Lite (Tables 27 and 28), solver results (Table 13 and Table 18), and individual proof attempts (Figures 7 to 12).

Appendix H describes the Lite task selection and result sets. Appendix C documents the statement-fidelity and result-validation checks.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendices list the task catalogue, agent configurations, proof and solver details, and per-attempt results.
